articles.title: DeSantis: ‘Florida will provide asylum’ to holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy case
articles.summary: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) on Friday accused the media of launching a smear campaign against the lone holdout juror in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial, after a report revealed that the juror had a history of alleged domestic violence and an active restraining order. “A man objected to allowing a woman to kill her…
articles.body:
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) on Friday accused the media of launching a smear campaign against the lone holdout juror in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial, after a report revealed that the juror had a history of alleged domestic violence and an active restraining order.

“A man objected to allowing a woman to kill her three young kids and get away with it, so NBC is trying to smear that juror, whose identity should be protected,” DeSantis wrote on social media in response to the report from NBC10 Boston . “Another low for legacy media.”

DeSantis went further as to offer the unidentified juror “asylum” in Florida should he face harassment over the bombshell revelations.

“If the juror is being harassed, Florida will provide asylum — I’m sure he’d be welcomed and appreciated,” DeSantis wrote.

NBC10 Boston reported Friday that the juror was charged in 2021 for allegedly assaulting his then-wife after his 13-year-old nephew told police he saw the man grab her by the throat and throw her into the dresser. The charge was later dismissed, and the couple divorced.

That same nephew obtained a restraining order against the juror last year after accusing him of pushing him onto the ground and assaulting him. The order was still active when the juror was selected for Clancy’s trial.

The findings raised questions about how the man was selected for the jury. Massachusetts’ standard juror questionnaire asks prospective jurors whether they have been arrested, charged with a crime or served with a court order.

NBC10 reported that each question would have applied to the juror, though his questionnaire is not public and it is unknown how he answered.

The outlet also reported that the juror was facing eviction after failing to pay rent since March. His landlord secured a judgement of more than $12,000 in unpaid rent while the jury was deliberating, according to the report.

The juror was the sole holdout after the panel split 11-1 on whether to find Clancy not guilty due to mental disease or defect. Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial last week after seven days of deliberations.

Clancy was charged with killing her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3 and Callan, 8 months — at the family’s Duxbury, Mass., home in 2023. Her attorneys argued she was experiencing postpartum psychosis and was not criminally responsible at the time of the murders.

articles.title: Trump says he would be OK with China building cars in the U.S.
articles.summary: U.S. automakers have urged Trump, who is due to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington this month, not to allow Chinese automakers access to the U.S. market.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump said on Friday he would not oppose Chinese automakers building cars in the United States despite widespread opposition from U.S. lawmakers and car companies. “If China wanted to come in and open a plant to build their cars here, I’d be OK with that,” Trump said in an interview on the Fox News program “The Ingraham Angle.” “Japan does it, but they hire our people. The big thing is they hire our people,” he said. He added that he does not want Chinese automakers to build cars in Mexico and ship them to the United States. “I’m not knocking Chinese cars,” Trump said. U.S. automakers have urged Trump, who is due to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington in two weeks, not to agree to allow Chinese automakers access to the U.S. market. On Wednesday, U.S. Senator Elissa Slotkin, a Michigan Democrat, said there were “rumors that Trump is planning to allow Chinese cars to be sold in the U.S., as part of a larger deal he’s putting together. That would be a strategic mistake.” Trump called Slotkin’s statement a “total phony rumor” and said he had kept Chinese vehicles out of the United States. A regulation imposed by former President Joe ​Biden’s administration in early 2025 effectively bans all Chinese automakers from selling or building passenger vehicles in the U.S. Washington also maintains more than 100% tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles. Last week, a group representing nearly all major automakers urged Congress to quickly pass legislation permanently barring Chinese vehicles from the U.S. market. The Alliance for Automotive Innovation, which represents General Motors, Ford, Toyota, Volkswagen, Hyundai, Honda, Stellantis and others, called for passage of the bill by the end of December. “Right now, Chinese automakers are dumping subsidized vehicles with connected software and hardware around the world,” the group’s CEO, John Bozzella, said in a letter to congressional leaders.

articles.title: Putin links AfD success in German state vote to mistakes by the West
articles.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin has linked the strong performance of Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the recent state election in Saxon...
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin links Germany's far-right AfD party's success in Saxony-Anhalt state election to mistakes by Western countries.

Putin accuses European governments of provoking conflict with Russia and unsettling citizens, suggesting this influenced election results in Germany.

Putin denies Russia poses a threat to European countries, arguing that conflict is being driven by European nations wanting to revise the outcomes of World War II.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has linked the strong performance of Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the recent state election in Saxony-Anhalt to mistakes by Western countries.

Everything currently happening in Europe was the result of systematic mistakes by Western states in politics, security and the economy, Putin said during a meeting with journalists in New Delhi.

He also accused European governments of provoking an open conflict with Russia and unsettling their citizens, suggesting this was reflected in election results in Germany.

The AfD garnered a record 43.8% in the vote on Sunday, falling just short of an absolute majority.

People in European countries understood what was happening, Putin said, adding that he believed this was also behind the results in Germany.

Putin is currently in India for a BRICS summit this weekend.

Kremlin-aligned television correspondent Pavel Zarubin published a video on Telegram in which Putin's remarks could be heard.

The Russian president had been asked to comment on the AfD's result in the Saxony-Anhalt state election. Putin responded at length, setting out his view of the situation in Europe.

Russia did not threaten European countries and had no grounds for a conflict with them, Putin said, arguing that all such issues had been settled by the outcome of World War II.

However, before Russia's invasion of Ukraine, Putin had also said that Moscow was not planning a war.

Instead, Putin suggested that the conflict was being driven by European countries.

"Do they want to revise the results of World War II? What are they pushing the people of their countries towards? A war with the Russian Federation?" Putin said.

"They are now talking about considering how they could send troops to Ukrainian territory. That means war with Russia."

articles.title: ‘War on terror’: How 9/11 changed the language of conflict
articles.summary: The events of September 11, 2001 spawned a new lexicon which effectively sanitised the erosion of human rights.
articles.body:
Torture became “enhanced interrogation”. Suspects were seized and removed across borders through “extraordinary rendition”. Detainees held at Guantanamo Bay were designated “enemy combatants”, while deadly attacks were described as “surgical” or “targeted” strikes.

In the years after the September 11 attacks on New York City’s World Trade Center, a whole new vocabulary of war, laced with the language of bureaucracy and precision, moved into the political mainstream in the United States.

At its centre was a phrase broad enough to encompass almost everything that followed: the “war on terror”.

That phrase came to define an era in which the US illegally invaded Afghanistan and Iraq, established the notorious Guantanamo Bay holding centre for “terrorists” and dramatically expanded its surveillance and national security powers at home. And it was all facilitated, experts say, by a new lexicon, one that sanitised violence, and erased the humanity of its targets.

Twenty-five years later, the phrase “war on terror” is now heard far less frequently from the White House. But many of the themes and ideas it helped to embed remain deeply rooted in US politics.

“I think we can see the legacy of the war on terror everywhere in US politics today,” Leonie Jackson, a senior international relations lecturer at Northumbria University in the United Kingdom, told Al Jazeera. “In fact, I would argue that we are still very much inside the logic of this ‘war’.”

Nine days after the attacks on New York and Washington, DC in 2001, then-US President George W Bush addressed a joint session of Congress. “Our war on terror begins with al-Qaeda, but it does not end there … It will not end until every terrorist group of global reach has been found, stopped and defeated,” he declared.

Congress had already passed the Authorisation for Use of Military Force, signed by Bush on September 18. The authorisation gave the president broad authority to use force against those he determined had planned, authorised, committed or aided the September 11 attacks, or anyone who had harboured those responsible.

But unlike a conventional war, this was not a war against a specific group or country.

“Terrorism is not a state, a territory or even a specific organisation. It is a tactic,” Christopher Baker-Beall of Bournemouth University told Al Jazeera.

“Declaring a ‘war on terror’, therefore, created a conflict without an obvious geographical boundary or clearly defined enemy and therefore, importantly, no natural endpoint.”

Later that year, Bush laid down a stark challenge for the international community: “Either you are with us, or you are with the terrorists.” Bush also frequently used the term “evil”.

Harmonie Toros, professor of politics and international relations at the University of Reading in the UK, told Al Jazeera that this “language is used to sanitise actions taken by the US – actions that could be seen as not okay for a normal, functioning democracy to undertake”.

At the same time, she said, it represented “a strong discursive effort to demonise” the enemy. Fear, anger and the desire to respond, Toros said, “come together and create this ‘war on terror’”.

The result was a narrative that divided the world not only between allies and enemies, but between notions of “good” and “evil”.

In his paper, 9/11, the Crisis of Meaning, and Disinformation in the 21st Century, Jason Thomas wrote that this stems from colonial ideas of civilisation and barbarism, and the US had constructed a narrative that “asserted the … ‘civilised/barbarian’ as a fundamental axis in world politics”.

When torture became ‘enhanced interrogation’

The US invaded Afghanistan less than a month after the events of September 11, 2001. Then, in March 2003, a US-led coalition invaded Iraq based on repeated claims by the Bush administration that Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein possessed weapons of mass destruction that could threaten the US and its allies. In the end, the stockpiles Washington said it was certain existed were never found, but by that time it was too late.

The “war on terror” quickly expanded into a sprawling network of global military operations and covert operations.

Nearly 780 people would eventually pass through the US military prison at Guantanamo Bay. All but a handful have since been freed without ever being charged with a crime, but some had by then languished in detention without charges for two decades .

When the British-American human rights lawyer Clive Stafford Smith first arrived at Guantanamo to render legal aid to detainees there shortly after it opened – he was among the first lawyers to be granted access – he said he saw boys as young as 14 being held. “The Guantanamo detention camp was born a sorry lie and it remains one,” Stafford Smith wrote for Al Jazeera in 2022.

Besides Guantanamo, the CIA operated secret detention facilities, or “black sites”, overseas while the abuse and torture of prisoners by US forces at Abu Ghraib prison in Iraq became one of the defining scandals of the war.

Oiling the wheels for those practices was a language that often appeared deliberately clinical. Torture and abusive interrogation methods including the notorious practice of waterboarding, prolonged sleep deprivation and stress positions were described as “enhanced interrogation techniques”. The covert transfer of detainees outside ordinary judicial processes became “extraordinary rendition”.

“What is striking about many of these terms is their bureaucratic or technical character,” Baker-Beall said. The effect was to create “moral and political distance” which “can sanitise acts of extraordinary violence and turn them into something that sounds like an ordinary instrument of government policy”.

In a series of legal memoranda which became known as the “Torture Memos”, lawyers in the Bush administration constructed an extraordinarily narrow interpretation of what constituted torture as the CIA sought legal authority to use increasingly brutal and coercive interrogation techniques.

Jackson said euphemistic language helped cloak such practices in “a veneer of legality”, allowing leaders to violate international legal protections, while maintaining the image of the US as the “good guys”.

Tahir Abbas, professor of criminology and global justice at Aston University in the UK, told Al Jazeera “this language also desensitised ordinary members of the public, rendering them increasingly numb to the deeply dehumanising and depersonalised ways in which death and destruction were discussed”.

“Often in relation to innocent victims,” he added.

Forty-five days after September 11, Bush signed the Patriot Act, vastly expanding the surveillance apparatus of the US government and making it easier for intelligence and law enforcement agencies to share personal information.

The post-9/11 security architecture also transformed the way immigration, borders and domestic policing were understood. The Department of Homeland Security was established in 2002, bringing numerous agencies responsible for borders, immigration, transport and security under a single national security structure.

Security policy became increasingly concerned not simply with what somebody had done, but with what they might do.

“The key political shift went from responding to actual threats towards governing possible future threats,” Baker-Beall said. “Once that happens, the potential scope of security policy becomes much wider.”

That logic created political space for intelligence gathering, detention, border controls and executive power. Governments across Europe also introduced sweeping counterterrorism laws and expanded surveillance, while Muslim communities increasingly found themselves on the receiving end.

Abbas described the result as a “boomerang effect”, in which citizenship stripping, securitisation and surveillance became normalised in the lives of Muslims.

The language of the war on terror, he said, helped build a wider politics of “othering”, in which entire communities could be cast as sources of danger – making mere suspicion itself a justification for surveillance, detention and other forms of state control, even when individuals had done nothing wrong.

By the time Barack Obama became US president in 2009, the new terminology had begun to change. On 23 May 2013, Obama announced that the “war on terrorism” was over.

But the institutions built in the wake of September 11 did not disappear with it. US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, was created as part of the Department of Homeland Security, its enduring legacy being increasingly frequent images of ICE agents patrolling streets in balaclavas arresting people of colour and assaulting protesters since Donald Trump began his second term as US president last year.

Far from being shut down, Guantanamo Bay – itself perhaps the most recognisable physical symbol of the post-9/11 suspension of ordinary legal norms – has been used by the Trump administration to detain migrants.

The war on terror, therefore, left behind a legacy of constructing threatening communities: “a practice of villainising a specific group of people”, Toros said.

“It can be gangs or a specific immigrant group, or even gender or gender identity. Post-9/11 and all the war on terror discourse allowed people to become more skilled when the intent is to villainise a community.”

And its legacy expands into US foreign policy, with Trump ordering the executive branch in 2025 to use the name “Department of War” as a secondary title for the Department of Defense, saying that the name better conveyed America’s willingness not simply to defend itself but to fight and win wars.

And those ideas have played out on Trump’s watch. The US is once again at war in the Middle East , with Trump claiming that military action against Iran was necessary to prevent it from developing a nuclear weapon – a justification that has drawn comparisons with the claims about weapons of mass destruction used in the run-up to the invasion of Iraq in 2003.

The Trump administration has also drawn on parts of the post-9/11 lexicon while developing a vocabulary all of its own. Military action has again been framed through the language of “pre-emptive” and “precision” strikes, while Iran has repeatedly been described as a “terror regime” and the “world’s leading state sponsor of terrorism”.

“It is not simply a continuation of the ‘war on terror’ and the circumstances are very different,” Jackson said. “But the same pre-emptive security logic is familiar.”

“What is striking is the continuing power of the same political argument: We cannot afford to wait for the threat to materialise, so action has to be taken now.”

She added that “the legacy of the war on terror everywhere in US politics today”.

“We may have moved away from the language of the war on terror, but its effects remain deeply ingrained in US society.”

articles.title: The Memo: Trump’s convention may struggle to turn tide for GOP
articles.summary: President Trump basked in the approval of the MAGA base during this week’s Republican midterm convention in Dallas. But the bigger question is whether the event made any difference to a political landscape that is seriously challenging for Republicans as Election Day looms less than eight weeks away. The Hill’s data partner Decision Desk HQ…
articles.body:
President Trump basked in the approval of the MAGA base during this week’s Republican midterm convention in Dallas.

But the bigger question is whether the event made any difference to a political landscape that is seriously challenging for Republicans as Election Day looms less than eight weeks away.

The Hill’s data partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) on Friday gave Democrats a 68 percent probability of taking control of the House, with control of the Senate — once considered relatively safe for the GOP — a 50-50 split. Virtually no significant polling has been conducted since the Republican gathering, however.

By Friday, it was notable how swiftly the national news agenda was moving on from the GOP convention. Instead, commemorations marking the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, were the focus of attention.

The most significant news from the Dallas event was Trump’s pledge to send a $5,000 “dividend” to every adult American citizen if Republicans win the elections in November.

But there are massive questions around this — even beyond the charge that it is, in essence, adjacent to bribery.

First of all, Trump has a record of making comparable pledges of windfalls from tariffs and from savings ostensibly made by the Elon Musk-led Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).

None of those promises has materialized.

On Thursday evening, Trump lashed out angrily at a reporter — Rachel Scott of ABC News — when she began asking a question about his track record in this respect. The website The Bulwark, often a locus of Trump criticism, compiled several clips of his past pledges.

Even among some Republicans, reaction has been lukewarm at best. A back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests Trump’s plan would cost roughly $1.3 trillion — and at a time when the national debt is already over $40 trillion and the global bond markets are getting antsy about the state of the federal government’s finances.

Vice President Vance notably did not mention the proposal during his keynote address on Thursday night, though he had defended it when asked during a Fox News interview the previous evening.

On the same network, Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) said his opinion of the idea would depend “on how it’s structured,” and that he favored a tax refund for people who are employed. “I don’t think we should be paying people that are not working,” he said.

Other Republicans were even more equivocal. Rep. Pat Fallon (R-Texas), also speaking on Fox News, said “President Trump isn’t saying that if we win we’ll do this. He’s saying we’ll be in a position to do this.”

But Trump took to social media on Friday to insist it would happen . “When I say something, I mean it!” he claimed.

Republican pollster David Winston cautioned against reading too much into the way other GOP members reacted, given that it appears few had advance notice of the proposal Trump unveiled.

“Part of the reaction you are hearing is that people are unsure,” Winston asserted. “They’re not saying it’s good or bad. When something like that gets dropped on you, you want some time to think through it.”

But others took a harsher view — including some Trump-skeptical Republicans.

Rick Tyler, a veteran GOP strategist who is often critical of Trump, called the dividend proposal “a gimmick,” adding “they don’t mean it.”

“I struggle with the level of sophistication of people thinking, ‘I’m going to get $5,000 if I vote for the Republicans,” Tyler said.

The broader political question over the Republican convention concerns the wisdom of making Trump so central to the party’s strategy heading into November.

The fundamental problem is Trump is significantly unpopular in the nation at large.

The DDHQ polling average on Friday afternoon found the president’s job performance eliciting disapproval from 57 percent of Americans and approval from 40 percent. Data analyst Nate Silver has Trump performing a few points worse, with just 38 percent approval.

Trump, as usual, proclaims enormous confidence. “Pretend I’m on the ballot,” he has said several times.

Democrats, however, are more than happy for Trump to be front and center.

“If Republicans in swing districts want to appear with Donald Trump, let the chips fall where they may,” Democratic strategist Julie Roginsky told this column.

“I understand they are trying to get as many MAGA voters as possible, but I think even those voters who will turn up for Trump will not, at this point, turn up for Republicans in a midterm election. So I just think aligning yourself with Trump is political suicide,” Roginsky added.

Tyler reached a similar conclusion, but from a different route.

The GOP strategist contended that there are indeed some times when it makes sense for a party to nationalize a midterm election.

He cited the success enjoyed by Republicans back in 1994, when their-whip Newt Gingrich (R-Ga.), unveiled a “Contract with America.”

But, Tyler added, “when you are the party in power and affordability is the number one issue and not getting better, it is not the time to nationalize the election. It’s the time to localize the election, and make the election about the opponent and what would happen if the opponent got elected.”

He contended that the event in Dallas “did precisely the opposite. It highlighted ‘we are the people in charge, we’re the ones you’re not happy with.’”

Some Republicans argue that, for all the coverage the convention created, it is substantive factors like the economy and the war in Iran that will ultimately determine the outcome of the midterms.

Winston, the pollster, argued that Republicans still have time to turn things around.

“The key moment would be when someone can walk into a grocery store and think, ‘’I am better able now to handle these prices,’” he said. “That could happen anytime up until Election Day. Somebody could walk into a grocery store on the last day of October and have that thought.”

As a hypothetical, that may be true. But Trump’s approval ratings on inflation are especially poor, and new data released on Friday showed the annualized inflation rate unchanged at 3.4 percent.

If things are going to change for Trump and the GOP, they need to do so soon — regardless of the claims made from the stage in Dallas.

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: McConnell’s return shines spotlight on older lawmakers
articles.summary: Sen. Mitch McConnell’s (R-Ky.) expected return to the Senate next week is drawing attention again to the health of aging lawmakers. He has since been recovering at home and engaging in what he described as…
articles.body:
Sen. Mitch McConnell’s (R-Ky.) expected return to the Senate next week is drawing attention again to the health of aging lawmakers.

McConnell, 84, was hospitalized over the summer for nearly two months after falling at home and receiving treatment for pneumonia. He has since been recovering at home and engaging in what he described as an “intensive regimen of physical therapy.”

His extended absence and advanced age have reignited conversations about lawmakers staying in office too long, with polls showing many voters support term limits, even as they also keep reelecting elder statesmen.

McConnell was first elected to the Senate in 1985 and is the 10th longest-serving senator in U.S. history. He is not seeking reelection to his current term, which ends in January.

Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D) has repeatedly raised questions over whether McConnell is fit to serve because of his health challenges this summer.

“I hope that he is one of the reasons that we get term limits. I’ll tell you what, I’d even name the bill after him,” he told CNN.

Iowa’s 44-year-old Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Rob Sand, has voiced his support for both age and term limits.

“The idea is, I want term limits. I want age limits. Let’s go get them,” he told reporters in April.

Compounding these arguments is the recent spate of lawmakers who have died in office, six in this term alone. Reps. Raúl Grijalva (D-Ariz.) Gerry Connolly (D-Va.) and David Scott (D-Ga.) were a decade or more past the typical retirement age of 65. Sen. Lindsay Graham (R-S.C.) was 71 when he died in office in July from aortic dissection a sudden condition that is not typically screened for.

In 2023, 90-year-old Sen. Dianne Feinstein (D-Calif.) died while in office.

Rep. Kay Granger (R-Texas) had left office just over a year before her death last month at age 83. The end of her tenure was marred by the revelation that she had been residing in a senior living facility and experiencing what her son Brandon Granger described at the time as “dementia issues.” Her family confirmed her death was caused by complications from Alzheimer’s disease.

Support for term limits on Congress remains overwhelmingly popular among Americans across the political spectrum.

An NPR/PBS News/Marist Poll released in May found that 83 percent of U.S. adults support term limits, with self-identified Republicans showing the highest rate of support at 89 percent. The same survey found that 80 percent of Americans also support an age cap on congressional candidates.

According to Aaron Dukette, senior strategist for the nonpartisan advocacy group U.S. Term Limits, support for imposing term limits has “skyrocketed” among Congress members in the past few years.

“We have 130-plus people who have signed a pledge and gotten on as co-sponsors for our amendment. So, it’s not obviously at the two-thirds threshold that you need to have both chambers, but it’s certainly growing,” Dukette told The Hill. “And I think people on both sides of the aisle started to recognize that this is something that’s going to benefit our whole electoral process and not just one party over the other.”

The joint resolution supported by his organization proposes limiting U.S. senators to two terms and House members to three terms. The version introduced in the House last year has 115 co-sponsors, 107 of whom are Republicans.

Although conversations and support for term limits and age limits persist among the general public, the discussions are rarer among lawmakers themselves, according to those who’ve worked with them.

Rodney Whitlock, managing director of Cozen O’Connor Public Strategies, was health policy adviser to Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) until 2015. Grassley, 92, is now the oldest member of Congress and was among the oldest when Whitlock last worked for him more than a decade ago. Grassley ranks as the longest-serving U.S. senator currently in the chamber, exceeding McConnell’s tenure by four years.

“It is not as common as one would think, unless the member starts to have issues,” Whitlock said when asked whether lawmakers and their staff talk about age.

He argued that the issue of an aging workforce is a broad one.

“Nobody should be looking at this going, ‘This is a unique problem to members of Congress.’ No, it’s not. It is societal. It is our issues with aging. All of these things are part of this conversation,” said Whitlock. He noted that during his time as a congressional staffer, views on aging lawmakers were more respectful, but the discussions have since become “overtly political.”

While describing that Grassley sees public service as a “calling,” Whitlock said there are “certainly” lawmakers who stay in office simply because they have “grown so accustomed to the lifestyle.”

Discussions about American gerontocracy encompass all branches of government. President Trump, 80, is the oldest person to be sworn in as U.S. president; former President Biden became the oldest sitting president, leaving office at 82.

At the Supreme Court, five out of eight sitting justices are past age 65; Justice Clarence Thomas is the oldest at 78.

Dukette from U.S. Term Limits said his organization is focused on limiting congressional service based on terms over age, reasoning that limiting terms would naturally resolve the age issue.

“We understand the concern and the desire for age limits, given the fact that we have many prominent elderly members of Congress that are running into health troubles while still being in office and they go … missing for a time,” said Dukette. “If it wasn’t for the 20, 30, 40-year careers that put them in that place in the first place — most members that run for Congress don’t start doing so in their 60s or 70s. They do so in their 40s or even in their 50s, and then they’re there for decades of service.”

When reached for comment on his condition and expected return, McConnell’s office referred to the senator’s last public statement released at the start of August, in which he said he would “continue my recovery at home” and “continue to engage with my staff and colleagues on important Senate business.”

The Hill has reached out to Grassley’s office for comment.

articles.title: Pennsylvania lawmaker suggests Trump should rename Lake Erie to 'Lake Pennsylvania'
articles.summary: Pennsylvania state Rep. David Maloney wants President Donald Trump to rename Lake Erie to "Lake Pennsylvania," following recent name changes to other bodies of water.
articles.body: Pennsylvania state Rep. David Maloney, a Republican, is asking President Donald Trump to rename Lake Erie to "Lake Pennsylvania" following similar renaming efforts by the president. Maloney is preparing a resolution calling on Trump, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and lawmakers on Capitol Hill to take steps to rename Lake Erie to "Lake Pennsylvania," arguing that the change is needed to reflect the lake’s modern identity. "This is Pennsylvania’s only Great Lake. Its modern economy and identity are increasingly tied to the boaters, anglers, families and tourists who come to enjoy it," Maloney said in a statement. "Ohio has plenty of shoreline. New York already has two Great Lakes. Canada has four others." NEW YORK GOV HOCHUL REJECTS TRUMP'S 'LAKE AMERICA' RENAMING WITH BLUNT MESSAGE "Pennsylvania has one. Let’s call it Lake Pennsylvania!" he added. Lake Erie is the smallest of the Great Lakes by volume as well as the shallowest, according to the Environmental Protection Agency. The lake has about 12 million people in its watershed, with 10.5 million people in the U.S. and 1.9 million people in Canada. This comes after Trump signed an executive order last month to rename Lake Ontario to "Lake America," a rebranding that Canada does not recognize and has firmly rejected. "We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always," Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement. SOUTH PARK CREATORS MOCK TRUMP'S LAKE ONTARIO RENAME AND COMPANY COMPLIANCE IN MOCK STATEMENT The renaming only applies to the U.S. federal government, meaning Canada, other international bodies and U.S. states are not forced to acknowledge the change. But both Apple Maps and Google Maps changed the name of Lake Ontario to "Lake America" for U.S. users following Trump's executive order. The president has also suggested renaming New Mexico to "New America," prompting several of the state’s Democratic lawmakers to call on Apple and Google to publicly commit to keeping the state's current name on their respective maps applications. Trump has also floated the idea of renaming the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans. On his first day back in office in January 2025, Trump signed an executive order to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the "Gulf of America," but, similar to the Lake Ontario rebranding, the order only applies to the U.S. federal government and does not bind Mexico, other international bodies or private entities. articles.title: Burnham and Badenoch revive red versus blue politics as Reform land £36m mega donation
articles.summary: As Reform slip back in the polls, Labour and the Conservatives rediscover a familiar political divide, writes Laura Kuenssberg
articles.body:
Look closely at the posters, placards and online posts. Your eyes aren't deceiving you if Labour's red seems a little deeper and the Conservatives' blue a little truer.

Politics seems to have found a new rhythm, one that feels a little familiar, despite Reform's jaw-dropping new donation putting it back in the headlines today.

For the avoidance of doubt, the scale of that £36m gift to Nigel Farage's party is like something from a different political universe.

"It's a gobsmacking sum," a senior figure involved in running successive election campaigns for one of the big parties tells me.

But one cabinet minister is enjoying what they see as a newly obvious difference between Labour and the Tories. "It's clarifying," they say, a clear gap between Labour and the Tories' "sense of purpose and values".

A member of Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch's top team tells me, "normal jogging is reasserting itself", hopeful they're at the start of a more straightforward, routine moment in politics after years of craziness, with smaller parties vying to shove the traditional tribes out of the way.

The standout moment was at the despatch box this week when Prime Minister Andy Burnham declared that national security couldn't come at the expense of social security - a phrase immediately seized on by the Tories, interpreting it as the PM saying he'd never cut welfare spending to pay for defence.

One senior conservative said: "It was a real line in the sand, we could never have imagined Sir Keir Starmer saying that."

The party seems cock-a-hoop at a line they can use again and again, asserting the prime minister cares more about welfare than guarding against war.

But there is a positive atmosphere in No 10 too, one source telling me that the face-offs between Badenoch and Burnham have "breathed new life into the Labour versus Tory dynamic".

How can they both be happy, when ultimately politics is a contest and there can only be one winner in the end?

Well, on the security spat, Burnham's backers are adamant he does want to cut welfare spending, and find more money for defence. How does that stack up with his words this week?

I'm told No 10 will explain in more detail his belief that security also means secure communities, which aren't created by slashing benefits.

Crucially, they reckon while cutting welfare might appeal to some voters, "once you dig into the 'who' and the 'how' of doing that, public support wavers, and when Kemi talks about housing benefit cuts, public opinion goes all over the shop".

They even cite that moment as evidence that the prime minister is "happy to grab thorny issues and put himself at the centre of them", as he did with the early release of prisoners.

He'll give a grabby-sounding view before the government has found a solution to a problem, stake part of his reputation on it, and make the case, hoping it will work out.

The choices are only going to get harder and harder though. "Hope" as a slogan and a strategy could never be enough.

But when politics is fundamentally a contest, how can both the traditional political tribes be buoyant?

For Labour, it's not just the obvious change of leader to a more effective politician who is much more at ease talking to the public, whether that's an eight-second TikTok or his long explanations of his positions expressed in a newspaper opinion piece and posted on Facebook.

It's that Burnham is making arguments that are more appealing to Labour's psychology – build council houses, take stronger action against the worst excesses of the Israeli government, stand up for those who need to rely on benefits from the state.

Labour believes, for now, they have a leader who is simply a better politician, who is making arguments many of them find instinctively more appealing.

The party knows what its leader believes, broadly at least. As one senior figure said: "He has a worldview which the last one didn't - he's clear what he wants and he's grabbed the reins of power."

Another who has worked under Starmer and now Burnham said: "It's just chalk and cheese."

And don't underestimate the importance of keeping backbenchers content, feeling understood. A government source joked the whips, the party managers, are becoming a bit "like an HR department" listening to concerns rather than driving the troops forward.

But as Starmer found to his cost, backbenchers weren't prepared to be loyal to him when many felt he hadn't shown much care or loyalty to them.

But Badenoch's tribe also seems more chipper because, as she has told friends, there is now a sharper ideological divide between the two parties saying, "it's much clearer to have those arguments rather than a process discussion with Starmer".

Shadow ministers reckon it's easier to make classic Conservative arguments because in the words of one, "Andy Burnham is a classic old leftie and we're the obvious answer to that".

Shock, horror, Labour sources I put that to dispute that is the case, one close ally calling him "a pragmatist", another denying he's further to the left than Starmer, because, "Keir was so hard to place".

But one conservative source also pointedly wonders how long Labour's happiness with their new leader will last, given Burnham's rapid return to Parliament saying, "looking at the benches opposite there is a vision of somebody who has turned up to a Tinder date and doesn't quite look like his profile pic".

Will this newly refreshed red-blue battle prove to be the real deal?

Rhetorical lines have been drawn this week, but real choices and arguments loom, and the bouncy feeling around the place may not last, especially when it comes to finding cash for the prime minister's big promises.

Downing Street sources acknowledge privately that bringing down the welfare bill in the way that Alan Milburn envisages, with his report expected, but not confirmed, to come before the Budget, will need billions spent up front, money the government might struggle to find.

Similarly, to build the council houses Burnham desires to cut the housing benefits bill will need big cheques.

It's one thing promising those Labour friendly dreams. It's another, perhaps at the party conference, to answer the much harder question of how the government plans to pay.

It won't be easy for a mid-term prime minister to find money in the short term that might only produce savings in the years to come.

But Burnham's Labour are happy to talk about the economy and how they want to help hard-up families, still citing the chaos of Liz Truss and keen to underline the early steps the prime minister has taken to ease the pressure.

With borrowing costs and the country's debt seriously sky high, the Conservatives are pleased to sketch out a classic left-right argument too.

It's also true they have both been enjoying the moment of real pressure on their opponents in Reform, who have slipped back in the polls, besieged by claims and counter claims about party funding.

Although this weekend's mega donation illustrates that Nigel Farage still has the capacity to bust political conventions. The money from the crypto billionaire , Ben Delo, is completely off the charts for our politics.

"To put £36 m in context, one man has donated a sum bigger than Labour's entire 2024 election budget, bigger than the Conservatives', and about six times what Reform actually spent," a senior figure told me.

"It's the kind of donation that could change how politics is funded in the UK."

During the last general election campaign Labour raised about £9m, the Tories, Reform and the Lib Dems all less than £2m.

These extra millions give Farage enormous and immediate spending power, and there might be more to come. Although you can bet the other parties will cry foul over the scale of this big money coming from men with deep pockets, not least because Delo was given an unconditional pardon by US President Donald Trump over violating the Bank Secrecy Act.

It would be daft for either of the two main parties to assume this apparent return to traditional two-party politics is here to stay. But it is strangely new to be in a moment when both Labour and the Conservatives are broadly content.

As the new prime minister's universe settles, a key Labour figure observed: "We've had the amuse–bouche and it was very tasty. What happens next?"

articles.title: Trump says he would 'love' to see Ireland unified as one nation
articles.summary: Trump says he would 'love' to see Ireland unified as one nation
articles.body: President Donald Trump said Saturday during a trip to Ireland that he would love to see the country unified. The Republic of Ireland gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1922, while Northern Ireland, established in 1921, has remained part of the U.K. "I don't want to cause any problems, but I will tell you, I'd love to see it unified. articles.title: For many Democrats this cycle, the tipping point between victory and defeat is Israel
articles.summary: Beneath their putative “big tent,” the national Democratic Party is embroiled in an ideological civil war — one that is likely to intensify through 2028’s presidential campaign.
articles.body:
Beneath their putative big tent, the national Democratic Party is embroiled in an ideological civil war that is likely to intensify through the 2028 presidential campaign.

While there are many topic Democrats disagree on — socialism, transgender issues, open borders and appeals to the white working class — the one that underlies this battle for the party’s soul is U.S. support for Israel.

“The genocide in Gaza has had an overwhelming effect on large, significant segments of the American public,” said Ian Lustick, co-author of the new book, “ Israel’s Lobby: America in the Grip of a Foreign Power. “ “Israel’s policies in the past 20 years have become essentially indefensible.”

For Jews critical of the Netanyahu regime, the horrific Oct. 7 Hamas attack (1,200 Israelis killed; hundreds taken hostage) did not justify killing thousands of Gaza civilians or targeting journalists and emergency medical personal with supposedly precision air strikes.

For single-issue, pro- Likud Jews, having a Democratic Party united against further U.S. aid to Israel means they would rather have a JD Vance or Marco Rubio in the White House, and a Republican-controlled Congress.

In U.S. Senate races in Michigan and Georgia, pro-Likud activists are supporting Republican campaigns.

Shocked by Abdul El-Sayed’s Democratic primary victory, prominent Detroit businessman Eric Bronstein — a Democrat — wrote an open letter to Jewish Democrats and independents in support of Republican Senate candidate and former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.). Several Jewish Democratic bundlers later met for a Rogers fundraiser.

Other Michigan Jewish Democrats, like Attorney General Dana Nessel, disagree, declining to endorse Rogers . “We have a moral imperative to place the needs of the world above even our own self-interest and, yes, even our own survival,” she told a gathering of Jewish Democrats, provoking Likud supporters’ outrage.

In Georgia, in an open letter to Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) — Jewish, up for reelection and a possible 2028 presidential aspirant — Atlanta Jewish Times publisher Michael Morris called on Ossoff to “stop lying to me and your constituents” about his “ironclad support for Israel. … Your antagonism toward Israel has remained steadfast.”

El-Sayed and Ossoff recently rejected controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker’s alleged antisemitic postings. That was insufficient and too late, legacy Jewish organizations said.

In Florida’s U.S. Senate primary, state Rep. Angie Nixon (D), a democratic socialist, has repeatedly accused Israel of committing genocide . She criticized the favorite for the nomination, Alex Vindman, for silence on Israel. She introduced a bill in the Florida legislature calling for a “de-escalation and ceasefire in the state of Israel and occupied Palestine,” supports cutting U.S. aid for the Jewish state and refuses AIPAC money. Nixon’s position on military aid to Israel helped her upset win .

Across the country, accepting AIPAC money has proved toxic for many congressional candidates. For decades, AIPAC threw its weight (and money) around with supplicants. But in insurgent primary campaigns this year, accepting AIPAC-sourced campaign money has become a liability.

Rogers’s campaign in Michigan is nervous, asking AIPAC to lie low and routing the cash from its superPAC, United Democracy Project, to a separate non-campaign group. Notwithstanding, Jewish Insider reports that Rogers attended four AIPAC fundraisers in Los Angeles over a long weekend in late August.

Even in deep-red Oklahoma, one candidate in the Senate Democratic primary ran a social media spot featuring a giant red bin labeled “AIPAC Funds,” with a caption reading, “ Just taking out the trash .” The candidate, N’kiyla Jasmine Thomas, trounced her pro-Israel opponent , centrist Jim Priest.

Of course, there are still some imponderable “ifs” ahead. If, for example, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is turned out of office in October, that may affect U.S. Israel supporters’ internal debates.

Ironically, approaching the fall midterms, Democrats are much less divided than current struggles over Israel would suggest. From the center-left Democratic governors of swing states who support Israel, like Pennsylvania’s Josh Shapiro , to progressives like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York City, consensus exists on November’s campaign agenda: economics, affordability, Medicare for All, higher federal minimum wage, free preschool and no AI data centers.

I have a modest proposal for Democrats: Put off this searing fratricidal controversy over Israel until after the midterms. Don’t fight over the spoils of victory until there is a victory to fight over.

Mark I. Pinsky is a journalist and author based in Durham, N.C. He was a civilian volunteer attached to the IDF in El Arish, Sinai, in the summer of 1967.

articles.title: What does ‘Never Forget’ mean for a generation with no memory of 9/11?
articles.summary: Pentagon 9/11 Memorial leader says new education center aims to connect generations with no memory of 9/11 to the facts and gravity of the attacks.
articles.body: Twenty-five years after a generation promised to "Never Forget," that pledge now relies on education for the more than 100 million Americans with no memory of 9/11/. The Pentagon is preparing to help address that challenge by breaking ground this weekend on a long-awaited Visitor Education Center at the only one of the three 9/11 attack sites still without a dedicated museum or education center. The new center is intended to fill the gap that has grown more pronounced with each passing year by helping Americans who never experienced the attacks understand not only what happened on Sept. 11, 2001, but why it continues to matter. Joseph Kornhoff, executive director of the Pentagon Memorial Fund, told Fox News Digital that nearly one-third of the country was either not alive that day or has no recollection of it and therefore lacks the "personal connection" shared by those who watched the attacks unfold. NEW 9/11 MUSEUM EXHIBIT AIMS TO CONNECT YOUNGER AMERICANS TO THE ATTACKS THROUGH POWERFUL ARTIFACTS "That's what we're trying to provide with the visitor education center experience," Kornhoff said in an interview with Fox News Digital, explaining that the goal is to give visitors a personal connection that allows them to "start to understand the gravity of that day." Nearly 230 miles north, the National September 11 Memorial & Museum in New York is confronting the same generational divide. Beth Hillman, president and CEO of the National September 11 Memorial & Museum, said the passage of time has only made the annual vow to "Never Forget" more important as the number of Americans with firsthand memories of the attacks declines. "Many in my generation remember exactly where we were on that horrific day," Hillman said during an Aug. 31 press preview outlining the museum's plans for the 25th anniversary. "Yet, 100 million Americans were not even born or are too young to remember that day for themselves today." BROOKLYN TEACHERS WHO WITNESSED 9/11 AS CHILDREN REVEAL WHAT THEY WANT THE NEXT GENERATION TO REMEMBER Noah Rauch, the museum’s senior vice president for education and public programs, said he has watched that transition unfold firsthand through the museum’s work with students and teachers. "I've seen this line creeping up between memory and history, between those who remembered the attacks and those who didn't," Rauch said during the Aug. 31 press event. That transition from memory to history also raises a more modern challenge. Americans too young to remember the attacks are increasingly learning about an event they never experienced firsthand, while conspiracy theories and false narratives about 9/11 run rampant online. Kornhoff said that makes factual education increasingly important, pointing specifically to conspiracy theories surrounding the attack on the Pentagon and narratives suggesting that America "deserved 9/11." "That's the need for the education center," Kornhoff told Fox News Digital. "As a nation, we need to really take a step back, look at how we're educating our young children to make sure that we're providing them with the facts of the situation ... and not these conspiracy theories and entertaining wild ideas that just simply are not true." REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: 9/11 IS JUST A HISTORY CHAPTER FOR A NEW GENERATION OF AMERICANS The Pentagon center will include 10 exhibits telling the human stories of the attack, including the 184 people killed at the Pentagon and aboard American Airlines Flight 77, the first responders who rushed to the scene and the military and civilian personnel who aided the wounded. "We are going to address the facts of the day," Kornhoff said. "We are going to address the entire Pentagon story." The renewed focus on 9/11 education has also reached Capitol Hill. Reps. Elise Stefanik, R-N.Y., and Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., introduced bipartisan legislation ahead of the 25-year anniversary, which aims to direct the Department of Education to examine how 9/11 is taught in schools nationwide and identify gaps in instruction. Kornhoff praised the effort during his interview with Fox News Digital, saying the legislation reflects a growing recognition of the need to educate generations with no firsthand connection to the attacks. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Pentagon 9/11 Memorial Visitor Education Center is expected to open by the end of 2029 near the existing Pentagon 9/11 Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery in Arlington, Virginia. The project received $12 million in federal funding this year, along with $1 million from Virginia and additional private donations raised by the Pentagon Memorial Fund. Once completed, the center is expected to include interactive exhibits, historic artifacts and firsthand accounts from survivors and victims' families while providing visitors with additional context about the attack and its aftermath.

articles.title: White House unloads on violent ‘criminal alien’ nabbed after investigators uncover election offense
articles.summary: Anthony Tyrone Higgs, a Bahamian green card holder with a violent rap sheet, was arrested after officials say he illegally voted in the 2020 election.
articles.body: A Bahamian national who arrived in the U.S. during President Gerald Ford’s administration and was living with a green card while racking up a violent rap sheet before investigators found he voted illegally in the 2020 election, sparking the deportation process, officials say. The case of Anthony Tyrone Higgs is only the latest in a slew of arrests connected to illegal votes cast in recent elections, as the Trump administration engages in a broader crackdown on election integrity-related crimes. "This alien was a guest in our country who forfeited his right to be in the U.S. when he committed these violent crimes and voted in the 2020 election," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis exclusively told Fox News Digital on Friday. ICE ARRESTS PERUVIAN NATIONAL ACCUSED OF ILLEGALLY VOTING IN 2024 ELECTION AS DHS CITES SIMILAR CASES "Any non-citizens who vote illegally in our elections will be arrested and removed. American elections are only for Americans." Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), a division of DHS, confirmed in a statement that Higgs had illegally voted in the 2020 election. FORMER KANSAS MAYOR WHO PLEADED GUILTY TO ILLEGAL VOTING TURNS HIMSELF IN TO ICE HSI’s Atlanta office arrested Higgs in Decatur, Georgia on September 3, and he is currently in the custody of ERO, the ICE subdivision that handles migrant removal operations. Higgs was admitted into the U.S. in October 1976 as a Lawful Permanent Resident – commonly dubbed a Green Card holder. The Trump DHS has since placed him in proceedings to revoke his immigration status due to his lengthy rap sheet. TRUMP DOJ UNLEASHES LARGEST DENATURALIZATION EFFORT IN DEPARTMENT HISTORY — AND SAYS IT’S ‘ONLY THE BEGINNING’ "This criminal alien from the Bahamas has a rap sheet for multiple violent crimes, including armed robbery, domestic violence, and assault on a police officer," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said. "On top of all of that, he illegally voted in the 2020 election," he added. MORE THAN A QUARTER-MILLION NONCITIZENS MAY BE REGISTERED TO VOTE IN 4 KEY STATES, DHS ALLEGES Higgs’ record also includes resisting arrest, two counts of grand larceny and two counts of possession of a weapon during a violent crime. Of the voting-related charge, Mullin said that just one noncitizen casting a ballot is enough to cancel out an American citizen’s vote. "Thanks to the hard work of the men and women of ICE, this criminal will be removed from our country and can never interfere in our elections again," he continued. DHS also provided several other recent cases of illegal immigrants or ineligible voters committing or being charged with election-related crimes. In August, Colombian illegal immigrant Carlos Jaramillo-Grajales was sentenced to three years in prison following an ICE investigation that led to a guilty plea in a case where he was found to have committed identity theft to illegally vote in elections for more than 20 years, according to the agency. "Federal immigration laws serve to safeguard our nation’s borders and protect the integrity of our government," said Gregory Kehoe, U.S. Attorney for the Middle District of Florida. "Those who seek to circumvent, exploit, or break these laws will be prosecuted fully," he said in an August statement. In New Jersey, a Slovakian national was found to have illegally voted in the 2022 midterms, according to HSI – which also cited the case of an Australian national accused of illegally casting ballots in both 2022 and 2024 in Louisiana. Mauritanian national Mahady Sacko was busted by an ICE and FBI partnership in Democrat-run Philadelphia, and charged with voter fraud. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Sacko allegedly voted illegally multiple times going back to 2008. He was already under an order of removal, DHS said in a statement, stating that he "exhausted all appeals" and an immigration board upheld his removal order as of 2002 but he remained in the country. articles.title: Democrats are within striking distance in the Senate, but shouldn't celebrate yet
articles.summary: Democrats are within striking distance of flipping the Senate, but razor-thin margins and candidate flaws in Texas, Michigan, and Maine loom large.
articles.body: If the 2026 midterms were held today, polls suggest that Democrats would be the favorites to retake the Senate. Indeed, according to RealClearPolitics polling averages, Democratic Senate candidates lead in North Carolina (+8%), Minnesota (+4%), Texas (+3%), Ohio (+3%), as well as Michigan, Maine, and Alaska (+2% each). Moreover, with President Trump’s approval rating hovering just below 40%, it’s legitimate to ask whether his sagging approval numbers will drag down Republican candidates across the country. 12 RACES SCRAMBLE SENATE BATTLEFIELD AS DEMOCRATS EYE COMEBACK Needing to flip four seats — assuming no GOP pickups in Michigan, Minnesota, or Georgia — the Senate is well within striking distance for Democrats, according to the data. That being said, the midterms are not today, and roughly two months until Election Day is a considerable amount of time. In that same vein, the Democratic candidates in these races have a number of personal and party-wide vulnerabilities, so it is by no means clear that what may currently look possible — or even probable — will come to fruition. TRUMP'S APPROVAL RATING PLUMMETS TO NEW LOW AHEAD OF CRITICAL MIDTERMS: 'MORE WORK TO DO' I say this for a number of reasons. First, outside of North Carolina and Texas, in each state, the Democrats’ polling advantages are well within the margin of error. Voters tend to turn their attention to midterms only after the summer ends, so it is entirely conceivable that these numbers reflect high-frequency voters, which often benefits Democrats. Second, and perhaps more important, frustration with the Trump administration will only get Democrats so far — candidate quality remains a deciding factor for many moderates and swing voters. LEE CARTER: THE SUMMER POLLS MISSED THE POINT: VOTERS ARE MOVING — AND THE MIDTERMS BEGIN The success of candidates affiliated with, or members of, the Democratic Socialists of America has opened a lane for Republicans to paint all Democrats as out-of-touch, far-left extremists. In 2024, then-candidate Donald Trump effectively painted former Vice President Kamala Harris as too far left on hot-button social issues, and Democrats have only moved further left since. DEMOCRATIC INFIGHTING GROWS AS CONGRESSWOMAN EXPOSES ‘DISRESPECTFUL’ WELCOME OF SOCIALISTS INTO ‘BIG TENT’ On this, races in Texas, Michigan, and Maine in particular will be crucial to watch and may represent Republicans’ best hope of maintaining control of the upper chamber. As I’ve noted previously in these pages, the Democrats in those races — James Talarico, Abdul El-Sayed, and Troy Jackson, respectively — are so far to the political left that it’s easy to see how voters could be turned off. SENATE MAP TIGHTENS AS TOP FORECASTER MOVES 3 RACES TOWARD DEMOCRATS Whether it’s Talarico’s past support for transgender women competing against biological girls in sports, El-Sayed’s anti-American statements, his rabid anti-Israel positions, his association with far-left Twitch influencer Hasan Piker, or Jackson’s history of flip-flopping and other controversies, these are flawed candidates. To that end, as these campaigns kick off in earnest, Republicans are all but certain to remind voters of their opponents’ far-left progressive positions on a number of issues. GOP SENATOR, EX-HOUSE DEM EMERGE FROM ALASKA’S ‘JUNGLE PRIMARY’ DESPITE FAR-LEFT MEDDLING Even when the Democrat is not a progressive, such as in Alaska, where Mary Peltola is a moderate Blue Dog Democrat, Republicans may be able to tie all Democrats to the DSA. That’s been Republican Dan Sullivan’s strategy, framing a vote for Peltola as a vote for a Senate hostile to the state’s energy sector — a vital local issue — despite Peltola’s record of supporting drilling. Third, on a basic level, Democrats’ task is made more difficult by needing to secure 51 seats given Vice President JD Vance’s tiebreaking vote and the possibility that Sen. John Fetterman could switch parties. He has repeatedly denied any intention of doing so, though his video appearance at the GOP convention in Dallas on Wednesday did nothing to quell rumors or speculation. Finally, Republicans have a sizable cash advantage. In recent filings, the Republican National Committee reported $128.5 million in cash on hand, versus $16.3 million for the DNC. FORMER DSA MEMBER ALLEGES COMMUNISTS HAVE ‘CAPTURED’ SOCIALIST GROUP, WARNS DEMOCRATIC PARTY IS NEXT Additionally, across the three major Republican committees and two affiliated super PACs, Republicans reported $657 million — nearly double the $334 million held by comparable Democratic groups. President Trump’s super PAC alone has more than $400 million. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Ultimately, Democrats have a genuine chance to retake the Senate, a remarkable achievement just two years after their 2024 across-the-board defeat. The 2026 Senate map had been considered favorable to Republicans, but, according to the polls, it’s Democrats who have the momentum. That Democratic candidates would be leading in Senate races in states like Alaska and Texas would have been inconceivable not long ago. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP However, the midterms are by no means a foregone conclusion, and a polling lead two months before Election Day is not the same as winning the election. Democrats’ razor-thin margins in the majority of the states they need, lingering concerns over candidate quality and the DSA’s impact, as well as Republicans’ massive financial advantage, mean it is by no means clear that the Senate will flip.
